newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: SOCIALISTS BACK IN POWER IN FRANCE
French President, Jacques Chirac's gamble in calling an early election has proved a huge mistake, with the Socialist opposition winning a near landslide victory.
President Chirac himself was not up for re-election, but he decided to call the poll a year early.
The people of France have sent him a clear message, with the centre-right government losing more than 240 seats in the national Parliament.
This means the Socialist Party's now in a position to rule without the help of its Communist Party allies.
The extreme right-wing National Front won just one seat.
LABOR STANDS FIRM DESPITE NATIVE TITLE ELECTION THREAT
The Federal Opposition says the Prime Minister must change his 10-point plan on native title if he wants to avoid a double dissolution election.
John Howard's expected to hold talks on the issue with Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, later this week.
The Opposition says if the plan involves "bucket-loads of extinguishment", as claimed by National Party leader, Tim Fischer, it won't work.
Labor says nobody wants a double-dissolution election, but if the plan is not changed to protect native title, it is prepared to go to the polls.
BHP "SHOULD CHANGE REDUNDANCY FORMULA FOR NEWCASTLE"
The Australian Workers' Union says many people who will lose their jobs at the Newcastle Steelworks in 1999 will be paid inadequate redundancy packages unless BHP changes the way they are calculated.
Union official Bob Williams says under the current system, workers will be given pay-outs based on their basic 38 hour week wage, even if they normally receive penalties or overtime.
Mr Williams says the union wants BHP to take shift work into account when it determines the amount a worker receives.
SA OPPOSITION PLEADS WITH PM FOR RAIL CASH
South Australian Opposition Leader, Mike Rann, has written to the Prime Minister, urging him to provide $300 million towards the Alice Springs to Darwin railway project.
Rann, who is in Darwin today for a Labor Party lunch, has asked John Howard to allocate part of the billion-dollar Federation Fund to the project.
He says the completion of the railway promised by the Commonwealth in 1911 is of vital importance in maximising Australia's trading opportunities in the coming century.
ALP WANTS INVESTIGATION INTO WAR-TIME SINKING OF SHIP
The Federal Opposition is pushing for a Parliamentary inquiry into the sinking of HMAS Sydney off the West Australian coast in 1941.
More than 600 lives were lost when the ship was sunk without trace and no survivors, by the German warship Kormoran.
Labor wants a Select Committee to examine the circumstances of the sinking, with reference to archival material from allied and former enemy forces.
It would also examine whether the Commonwealth Government should take part in a search for the ship.
The matter's expected to be debated in Parliament today.
GUN CONTROL GROUP WELCOMES NEW ADS
The Coalition for Gun Control has welcomed new advertisements for the firearms buyback scheme.
The ads advise gun owners of their entitlements and responsibilities under the scheme.
Rebecca Peters of the Coalition for Gun Control says the Government is right to portray gun owners as law abiding citizens who recognise the buyback is a good deal.
She says the 409,000 guns handed in represent a significant step towards a safer society, though the returns have been patchy in some states.
Owners have until the end of September to hand firearms in and take advantage of compensation.
Just over $206 million has been paid out to gun owners so far.
GOVTS TAKING, BUT NOT GIVING, ON DRUGS AND ALCOHOL
A report has found revenue to Australian governments from drug and alcohol taxes has risen by seven billion dollars.
But the Alcohol and Other Drugs Council of Australia report says spending on programs to combat drug and alcohol abuse fell to just A$160 million.
Council Chief Executive, David Crosbie, says the Northern Territory has the best record in Australia, while most other governments have failed to confront the drugs problem.
Crosbie says every dollar spent on treatment and prevention leads to a community benefit seven-to-ten times greater.
